USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the existing $50 billion Section 301 tariffs in place and do not rush to slam the proposed $200 billion List 3 at 25 percent the day after the comment period closed. Re-open a senior (Liu He-level) channel aimed at structural IP, forced tech-transfer, and market-access remedies—not another purchase-only truce. Treat unfinished List 3 coverage and rate as unused leverage; implement a narrower 10 percent list only if Beijing refuses to re-engage on those structural issues.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not high. The Section 301 record (22 Mar 2018) established discriminatory IP/tech-transfer practices; the May 19 joint statement then collapsed on 29 May when Washington concluded a purchase pledge was not a structural fix. Lists 1–2 are now live (25% on ~$50B as of 6 Jul and 23 Aug) and China has matched dollar-for-dollar, including soybeans, autos, and aircraft. That retaliation is already biting a key export sector: China bought nearly a third of U.S. soy in 2017, cash prices are down ~$2/bushel (~20% since June), and USDA on 28 Aug began $4.7B of a $12B farm package—political and sectoral pressure, not a national GDP shock. U.S. goods exports to China have slipped (EXPCH ~$10.5B in April to ~$9.3–9.7B in Aug/Sep) while imports from China have been front-loaded (IMPCH ~$38B to ~$50B), so the goods deficit has widened rather than closed. That is a cost of the current path, not evidence the strategy is working. Macro still argues against panic or maximal escalation: Michigan sentiment is 100.1, industrial production is rising, VIX is ~13.9, and CPI is only modestly higher. China is under more cyclical strain (IP slowing to 105.8, CNY weaker by ~8% to ~6.83, reserves down ~$37B). List 3 hearings had to be doubled to six days because hundreds of U.S. firms objected, and the 10%→25% rate hike floated on 1 Aug would pull in consumer and intermediate goods the first $50B deliberately avoided. Working-level Malpass–Wang talks in August were explicitly second-tier after the May collapse; they are not a settlement track. Escalating immediately would likely draw asymmetric Chinese replies (further CNY move, pressure on U.S. firms in China, deeper farm diversion to Brazil) into the harvest and midterms, while conceding or rolling back now would cash out unused List 3 leverage for nothing structural. Negotiating without new U.S. commitments, with $50B held and List 3 still on the table, is the stance that matches a modest threat and a still-favorable U.S. cyclical position.
key_factors: Section 301 IP/tech-transfer findings remain unmet; May purchase-only truce already failed
Matching $50B tariffs are live; soy and other farm exports are the main U.S. pain point
U.S. macro still strong (sentiment, IP, low vol); China showing FX, IP, and reserve strain
List 3 ($200B, 10% vs 25%) is in process, not yet imposed; hearings showed broad U.S. firm opposition
Talks have been downgraded to working level; no advanced settlement to justify rollback or purchase concessions

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions... Truce collapses.
List 1 tariffs take effect: US 25% on ~$34B of Chinese goods. China imposes matching ~$34B retaliation the same day.
At Trump's direction, USTR says it is considering raising the proposed List 3 rate from 10% to 25%.
List 2 tariffs take effect: US 25% on ~$16B (completing the $50B package). China imposes matching ~$16B retaliation.
U.S. consumer sentiment 100.1 as of 2018-09-01, up from midsummer.
U.S. goods exports to China down from $10.5B (Apr) to $9.3–9.7B (Aug/Sep).
U.S. goods imports from China up from $38.2B (Apr) to $49.9B (Sep)—front-loading.
CNY weakened from ~6.33 in March to 6.827 on 2018-09-05 (~8%).
VIX 13.91 on 2018-09-05; U.S. risk pricing remains contained.
USDA to pay $4.7B to farmers; >$3.6B to soy growers; ASA cites ~$2/bushel (~20%) price drop since June.
USTR doubled List 3 hearings to six days; 359 witnesses, mostly firms warning of higher costs.
August talks downgraded to Malpass–Wang; Kudlow called them second-level and warned China not to underestimate U.S. toughness.
